The session begins.

The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.

The lad stops so quickly that his rope sling swings forward. For a moment he looks surprised that anyone has asked his name at all.

"Tamsin, ser." He touches his brow, just under the small curled horns. "Directions, yes. Three coppers to the door, and I'll carry the pack for nothing if your shoulder gets tired on the hill. It's steep. People don't think it is, and then it is."

He glances up the slope, at the lantern-lit roofs, picking places out in his head.

"Decent and no fleas... the Elfsong, on Dragonspear Street. Clean sheets, the cook's honest, the Fist drink there and don't make trouble. It's dear, a few silver a night. Cheaper than that and you're sharing, with fleas or with people, and the people are worse." He shrugs one thin shoulder. "There's the Low Lantern too, a ship moored up as a tavern, but it rocks. Some don't mind."

When you lower your voice he leans in to match you, without seeming to think about it.

"The Lady's Hall is up top, behind the inner wall. Big place, gold on the doors. But the Upper City gates are shut by now, and the Watch won't open them for a man off a boat, not even to pray." He hesitates, then goes on. "There's the Lady's nook, though. Down here. A little niche in the wall by the Counting House steps, with her face carved over it. Clerks and dockhands flip a copper there before they go in to ask for a loan. Some say it helps. My mum says it's mostly how the steps get swept." He nearly smiles. "It's on the way to the Elfsong, near enough."

Behind you the line shuffles forward a pace. Sergeant Brannick's voice comes again, closer now: "Name. Business. Bed." Over by the warehouse door the cards slap down on the barrelhead, and someone curses cheerfully.

Tamsin waits with his hands folded on the sling's knot, polite and hopeful.

"And who am I taking up the hill, ser?"

"James," Tamsin repeats under his breath, the way a man files a coin in a pocket. "Done, ser. The nook, then the Elfsong." At the word *mum* his face shuts for half a second, politely, like a door pulled to. "She is sensible, ser. She'd tell you so herself." That's all he says about her.

The line moves, and then it's your turn at the trestle.

Sergeant Brannick doesn't look up for the name. "Worgen," he says, and his pen stops. "W-O-R?"

"G-E-N." The pen goes on, and this time he does look up, properly, at your face, your cloak and the cat at your boot. Then he looks back at the ledger.

"Work. Caravans are hiring. Ask at the Friendly Arm, or at the Fist hall by the Basilisk Gate if you can hold a spear and keep your mouth shut." He writes *Elfsong* beside your name. "Elfsong's good. Keep it that way. Next."

You're already stepping off when his left hand tears a thumb-sized strip from the bottom of a spare sheet. He copies something onto it in three quick strokes and slides it under the inkpot. Nobody else in the line got a strip.

The barrel by the warehouse door has gone quiet. Mirela Dask holds the deck squared in both hands and doesn't call to you a second time. She watches you go, the way you'd watch a dog you aren't sure of.

The hill is as steep as Tamsin promised. He goes ahead with his sling and picks the lit side of each lane. Twice he says "mind the gutter, ser" a step before there's a gutter to mind. Behind you a boy in a Fist tabard much too big for him runs past at a trot and turns uphill, east, towards the inner wall, holding something tight in his fist. Then he's gone round a corner.

The Counting House takes up a whole side of a small square: grey stone, iron-banded doors, two guards with halberds under a lamp. Your eyes are drawn up to one high window, still lit at this hour. A wooden bucket and a mop lean by a side door. Tamsin's eyes pass over them and don't stop.

The Lady's nook is at the foot of the steps, a niche a little taller than a man's forearm. Her face is carved above it, worn smooth by years of passing thumbs, and still smiling. A brass dish in the niche holds a scatter of coppers. In front of it one flagstone has been worn into a shallow bowl, the spot where people stand to flip.

The cat doesn't come to the nook. It has stopped three paces short, by an iron storm-grate set in the cobbles where the steps meet the square. It isn't moving. Its ears are pricked forward, its tail is low and still, and it's staring down through the bars into the black. Faintly, from somewhere far below, comes the sound of water.

"Here she is, ser," Tamsin says softly, and stands back to give you room.

Tamsin closes his fingers over the three coppers and looks at his own fist for a moment. Most people pay him later, or argue the price at the door, or don't pay at all. "Thank you, ser. That's early." The coins go somewhere inside his shirt. "Take what time you like. I'll be just here."

He steps back to the edge of the lamplight with the sling's knot in both hands, and for once he doesn't fill the quiet. His eyes drift to the side door with the bucket and the mop, then come back to the square.

You crouch. The grate is a square of iron bars a hand's width apart, rusted orange where they meet the frame. The cobbles around it have been worn smooth by feet that never stopped here. Below the bars there's black. The first few feet of slick masonry catch the lamplight, and then there's nothing to see. Cold air comes up past your face, carrying salt and wet stone and an older smell, the closed-in smell of a cellar nobody has opened in a long time. The water isn't trickling. It slaps slowly somewhere far down, against a wall, again and again, the way the harbour does.

The cat doesn't turn its head when you ask. What comes back through the bond isn't words. It comes as pressure.

*Down.*

Then a pull, the kind a cat feels from a mouse behind a wall: it can't hear the mouse, but it knows the mouse is there. *Under. There.* There's hunger in it, sharp and plain, the cat *wants*. Underneath the wanting there's something else, ears going flat in a way its real ears don't show: *don't like.*

That's all it has for you. It hasn't moved, except that its head has tilted a little. It isn't looking straight down the shaft anymore. It's looking down and slightly *toward the steps*, toward the grey wall of the Counting House and its iron-banded doors, as if whatever it wants lies under the building and not under the street.

Above you the high window is still lit. One of the halberdiers by the door shifts his weight and glances at the man crouched by a drain, then looks away again.

The Lady's nook waits at the foot of the steps, with her worn smiling face and the brass dish of coppers.

The cat's ears twitch when your thought reaches it. Through the bond comes a flat, sulky *no*, aimed at your request and not at the drain. It stays where it is, crouched at the grate, but it doesn't go any closer. After a moment it sits back on its haunches and wraps its tail around its feet, very tightly.

You stand on the worn flagstone, in the hollow that thousands of other feet have made. Up close the carved face is smaller than it looked, and the smile has nearly been rubbed away. It's still there, though, at the corners.

The copper goes up, turns over in the lamplight and comes down in the brass dish with a bright *tink*. It doesn't stay there. It hits the rim, hops out, drops to the flagstone on its edge and rolls. It goes out of the hollow in a slow, wobbling curve that runs away from you and away from the grate, across the cobbles, and stops against the foot of the first Counting House step. It tips over and lies flat, in the step's shadow, facing the iron-banded doors.

Under your hand the old coin on its cord is warm. It isn't warm the way skin warms metal. It feels like something set down in the sun for an hour, and then the warmth is gone.

Tamsin has watched it all from the edge of the light. "They mostly end up there, ser," he says, apologising for the square. "The whole place leans toward the doors. You can't see it, but rain runs that way. People's coppers too." He looks at the step, then quickly away again. "Nobody picks those up. It's bad luck, taking the Lady's change."

One of the halberdiers by the doors has followed the copper with his eyes. He looks at it, then at you, and then goes back to looking at nothing, the way a guard does.

Above the doors, the high window is still lit.

Tamsin shifts the sling on his shoulder. "The Elfsong's two streets up, ser, whenever you're ready."

The copper stays where it fell, flat in the shadow of the first step. You leave the Lady her change.

The cat takes its time about leaving. When you beckon, it gets up off its haunches slowly and stretches one back leg, then the other, as if it had meant to do that anyway. It falls in at your heel. Twice before the corner it stops and looks back at the grate. The second time its tail flicks once, sharply, and then it comes on.

Tamsin leads you out of the square up a lane of shuttered shops. There's a chandler's, a cooper's, and a sign with a painted boot on it. The halberdiers' lamp shrinks behind you to a yellow smudge. Here the hill steepens again, just as he promised, and the cobbles are older and set crooked.

When you ask, he doesn't stop walking, but his step goes short for a pace.

"Ser?" Then nothing for a few steps. He shifts the sling's knot from one hand to the other. He doesn't say *no*, and he could have. You watch him decide not to.

"My mum," he says finally, low, to the cobbles. "She does the floors there. Nights, after the clerks go. The halls and the stairs and the big room with the counters." He hurries on before you can say anything. "She's got proper work, ser. They pay her. She only mops, she doesn't go anywhere she isn't told, she's never been in any trouble with anybody." By the end it's coming out too fast, like something he's had ready for years in case anyone in a red tabard ever asked.

He glances at you sideways and quickly away. In the light of a doorway lamp his face is careful.

"I'd be grateful if you didn't say so to anyone, ser. People get ideas about our sort near money." He walks three more steps, then asks, very politely: "Why d'you want to know?"

Ahead, at the top of the lane, music and warm lamplight spill out across the street from an open door. Under the noise of the common room a woman's voice is singing, from somewhere you can't place.

Tamsin slows when you do. It takes him a few steps to trust it, the way a dog that's used to being hurried keeps glancing at the lead.

"Oh," he says. "No, ser. Nobody to worry about." He looks at the cobbles for a while. "The bucket's out, that's all. She leaves it by the side door when she goes in, so I know she's started and I don't need to wait for her."

When you ask if she's all right, he gives you a proper answer, the way people do when nobody has asked them in a long time.

"She's all right, ser. Tired. She does their floors from when the clerks go till the bell before dawn, and then she comes home and does ours. Her knees are bad from the stone, but she says stone's better than boards, because boards splinter." He nearly smiles, then stops himself. "Most nights the clerks are gone by ten bells. Lately there's someone up top later and later, and she has to wait out in the yard till they're done. They don't pay her for the waiting." He shrugs that off fast, like he's said something he shouldn't. "It's still good work. Better than the river."

He walks a few more steps.

"The Fist stop her sometimes, on the walk home. They ask where she's been at that hour." He says it flatly and doesn't go on.

The lane levels out at the top, and then the Elfsong is right in front of you. It's a tall old house with a sign of a painted elf-maid over the door, and lamplight and noise pour out of it. Somebody inside laughs loudly at a table. Under the noise you can hear the singing, clearer now. It's a woman's voice, high and sad, and it doesn't seem to come from anywhere in particular.

Tamsin stops on the doorstep and doesn't go in.

"Here you are, ser. Ask for Alan at the bar, he keeps the rooms. Tell him you want one at the back, the front ones get the street." He takes a breath, about to add something, then lets it go and fiddles with the knot of his sling. "Thank you for... well. Thank you, ser. I'm on the quay most mornings if you need anything carried."

He nods to you and gives the cat a small bow, which it ignores. Then he heads back down the lane, keeping to the lit side. At the bottom he turns left, away from the Counting House square, and disappears into the dark between the houses.

The cat sits on the Elfsong's step and washes one paw, and looks back down the hill at nothing in particular.

The door is open and the common room is warm. Nothing else is waiting on you tonight unless you go looking for it.

Place: The Elfsong Tavern · Time: Day 1 · night

The common room is wider than the house looks from the street, and the heat in it hits you at the door. A fire burns in a deep hearth on the left wall. A dozen tables are packed in under low black beams, with pipe smoke hanging between them. At a long table by the fire four Flaming Fist men sit with their tabards unlaced, playing at dice and talking more than they play. One of them glances at you, sees a cloak and a cat and nothing else, and goes back to his cup. Two women in good wool share a bottle in a corner and speak quietly in Chondathan. An old man sleeps upright on a bench under the stairs with his hat over his face.

The singing is clearer in here. It's the same high, sad voice, and it still comes from nowhere. Nobody in the room looks up at it, the way nobody looks up at rain on a roof. The cat's ears turn toward the ceiling, then toward the stairs, then back. After that it loses interest and slips under the nearest empty stool.

A bill is pinned on the post by the bar, a sheet of Baldur's Mouth gone soft with damp. The big black heading is about a Council levy on wharfage. Lower down, in smaller type, there's a short piece: *ANOTHER FROM THE GREY HARBOUR. The third this month. Coin found in the mouth. The Fist say drink; the fishwives say Umberlee.* Someone has drawn a little wave beside it in charcoal.

The man behind the bar is in his fifties. He's bald on top and has a clean apron and forearms like a cooper's. He's drying a tankard he plainly finished drying some time ago. He looks you over in one pass, your face, your boots and the cat under the stool, and sets the tankard down.

"Tamsin." He nods, as if that settles something. "He sends me quiet ones. I'm Alan. Rooms are mine, kitchen's my wife's, complaints go to whichever of us you like less."

He leans one hand on the bar.

"Back room's seven silver the night. Bed, a jug of water in the morning, a bolt on the door that works. It looks over the yard, so you'll hear the well and not the street. Supper's three silver. Tonight it's fish stew, brown bread, and an apple if you're lucky. Ale's four copper, wine's dearer and not better." He glances at the cat. "The cat sleeps where it likes so long as it keeps off the kitchen table. I've lost that argument with better cats than yours."

Up near the ceiling the voice climbs a note and holds it, then stops. In the quiet one of the Fist men says "*Gods*, there she goes," fondly, and the dice rattle again.

Alan doesn't look up. "That's Elf. She was here before me and she'll be here after. She doesn't take requests." He picks up the dry tankard again. "First night's paid up front. You want just the one, or are you staying the week?"

Alan watches the coins come down and counts them with his eyes before you've finished. Ten silver, four copper. He sweeps them off the bar into his palm without a word and drops them into a box under the counter.

"Worgen." He says it once, the way he'd chalk it on a slate. "One night. Supper, ale. Bolt works. You'll find out about the cat."

He takes an iron key on a loop of cord off a hook behind him and puts it on the bar in front of you. "Top of the stairs, left, all the way to the end. The door sticks in the wet. Shoulder it, don't kick it."

You ask about the Lady's Hall. He takes a moment over it, like a man working out the cost of a cart ride.

"Gates open at first bell. Go up clean and without the crossbow. The Watch stop a man with a weapon on his back, and they stop him longer if he talks like he's not from here." He nods at your rapier. "That on your hip, they'll look at it. They'll let it go if you're polite and going somewhere they like."

"Tell them you're going up for the morning toss. The priests flip a coin for the city at the Hall every morning, and half the Lower City climbs up to watch on a feast day. On an ordinary day it's a few dozen. The Watch are used to it, so it's the easy way through."

"Speaking to a priest is something else. You don't just walk up to one. There's a side door with an acolyte and a book. You give your name, leave something in the dish, and they find you a time. Leave a silver and they'll find you a time next week. Leave gold and they'll find one tomorrow." He shrugs. "I don't say that against the Lady. It's just how a big house runs."

He turns toward the kitchen hatch. "Hesta. One stew, back room."

A woman's voice answers from the steam, too low to make out. A minute later a bowl comes through the hatch: thick fish stew with the steam still rising off it, a heel of brown bread, and an apple, small and a little wrinkled but whole. Alan sets them in front of you with a tankard of ale, its foam already sliding down the side.

"You're lucky," he says, meaning the apple, and picks up the dry tankard again.

The cat comes out from under the stool, sits on the floor by your boot and looks at the stew, then at you. It makes no sound at all, and somehow that's worse than if it did.

Up near the beams Elf starts again, softer this time, a few low notes without words. At the fire table one of the Fist men loses a throw and swears at the dice, quite cheerfully.

Nothing else wants you tonight. There's supper, and a room at the end of the hall upstairs, unless you want something more from the evening.

"Don't say that too loudly," Alan says, without looking up from the tankard. "Hesta will put the price up."

The stew is better than the price suggested: thick with white fish and onion, and peppery enough to make the ale welcome. You set a flake of fish on the edge of the bread to cool and lower it to the floor. The cat looks at it as if it has been insulted. Then it eats it in three neat bites and goes back to waiting for more. When none comes, it gives up on you and starts watching the door to the street instead.

By the fire the Fist men are counting up their losses. Up in the beams, Elf has gone quiet.

The stairs creak at every second tread. The hall at the top is narrow and smells of beeswax and old wood, and the door at the far left end sticks exactly as promised. You put a shoulder to it and it gives with a damp groan. The room is small and clean: a bed with a grey wool blanket, a stool, a washstand with an empty jug, and a tallow candle burning in a dish on the sill. The shutter is open a crack onto the yard. Below it the well-rope creaks in its pulley when the wind takes it. The cat comes in on your heel, and the bolt slides home with a solid, well-oiled *chock*. Alan was telling the truth about that too.

You lay your papers out on the blanket by candlelight.

The promissory note is heavy paper, the kind a patriar's clerk uses, not a dockside scribe. It's cream-coloured and still crisp at the folds even after the voyage. The hand is young, and it hurries the way a man writes when the table is waiting on him:

*I, Peregrin Vane, of House Vane of Baldur's Gate, owe the bearer of this paper four hundred gold pieces, to be paid on presentation at the Counting House of Baldur's Gate, against the account of my House.*

Below that is the signature, *P. Vane*, with a flourish that has run out of ink halfway. A small blind stamp is pressed into the corner without wax: a weathervane, a little arrow on a crossed post, pointing nowhere in particular. Where the place and date should be, someone has set a wine cup down. A brown ring has eaten the line, and only *-ember* and a scrap of a number are left.

So it's the Counting House again.

The candle is behind the sheet as you tilt it to read the stamp. For a moment the paper isn't even. There's a paler patch in the middle of the weave, a shape the size of a thumbprint that's thinner than the rest. It's gone as you lower the page, and at this angle you can't make out what it was.

The cat jumps onto the bed. It treads a slow circle on the blanket the way cats do when they're choosing a place to settle, and stops on the edge of the note. It lifts the paw back off the paper as if the paper were wet. Then it steps around it, all the way around, and lies down on the far side of the bed with its back to the note.

A minute later it gets up again and goes to the shutter. It sits at the crack with its nose to the night air, facing downhill.

*(Out of game: I don't have an unfinished letter from your old company in James's things. Is that something from his past you'd like to add? If so, tell me who wrote it and roughly what it says, and it's in his pack.)*

You lift the sheet again and turn it slowly, keeping the edge a hand's width above the flame. The candle smokes a little. Light comes through the paper in a warm cream glow, and the ink of Peregrin Vane's hurried lines turns dark against it.

At one angle the pale patch is only a smudge in the weave. Tilt it a little further and it takes shape.

It's a face, about the size of a thumbprint, pressed into the body of the paper. Whoever made it put it there when the sheet was still wet pulp on the mould, not with ink. It's a woman's face, looking straight at you, set inside a thin ring of tiny raised marks, the way a face sits inside the rim of a coin. The work is fine. You can make out the line of her brows, the curve of her cheek and the shape of her mouth.

Her mouth turns down. Under each eye a short line runs across the cheek, thinner than a hair. The paper is translucent there, so in this light it shines. She is weeping.

The words *four hundred gold pieces* run straight across her face, with the ink stroke of *gold* passing between her eyes. The paper-maker can't have planned that. The clerk who wrote on it can't have known.

Behind you, at the shutter, the cat has turned its head. It doesn't come back to the bed. It watches the lit paper in your hands with its ears flat, and the bond carries one thing, sharp and short: *wrong.* Then it looks away, back through the crack toward the yard and downhill, and its tail wraps tight around its feet again.

The candle gutters in the draught from the shutter. The face goes faint and comes back. When you lower the page it's gone, and you're holding ordinary heavy cream paper with a wine ring in the corner.

Out in the yard the well-rope creaks once in its pulley. Somewhere below the Elfsong a dog barks twice, then stops.

The night is yours from here: the papers, sleep, or anything else, if you want it.

The answer comes, though not from anything you've seen on a temple wall.

It isn't the Lady. Nobody who serves Tymora shows her weeping, not in stone, not on coins, not in a chaplain's scratched drawing. Her face smiles or it's not hers. It isn't Beshaba either. The Maid of Misfortune's people don't carve a woman's face at all. Their sign is black antlers on red, and they don't put it on anything a respectable mill would make.

The lore you're remembering is older than both of them. Before the Time of Troubles there was one goddess of luck, not two. Tyche, the old priests called her. When the gods walked the earth she was split in two: Tymora came out of her smiling, and Beshaba came out of her bitter. Coins of Tyche's faith were struck with the same woman on both faces, fair on one side and foul on the other. Her people flipped them for their answers, and when they kept one as a charm they kept it smile-up. Old Tymoran clergy still talk about those coins like a family talks about a grandmother nobody mentions at the table.

So the face in Vane's paper looks like the bad side of that kind of coin. It's set inside a rim, the way a mint would strike it, and it's weeping.

What you don't recognise is the ring of marks around it. On a temple coin the rim would carry a prayer or the name of a mint. These look like neither: rounds and short strokes in no script you know, too regular to be decoration. A paper-maker pressed them into the mould on purpose.

The paper itself doesn't add up. A mill picks what goes in its moulds, and no patriar house would order the foul face of a luck-coin for its letters of credit. That leaves two possibilities: someone wanted it there, or nobody did.

The Coin of Tymora lies beside the note in the candlelight, worn and silver and cool now.

At the shutter the cat hasn't moved. Its nose is still at the crack and its tail still tight round its feet. Every so often one ear turns toward the door of the room and then back toward the yard, as if it's measuring how far it is to somewhere.

The candle has burned down maybe a finger's width since you came up. The night is quiet. Nothing else is waiting on you before sleep unless you want it.

One ear turns toward you and then back toward the yard. Something about *drains* gets a flick of the tail, and that's all.

The Copper Lanterns letter has been folded and unfolded so often that it's gone soft along the creases, like cloth. It's Dorna Hask's hand, small, square and leaning slightly backward, the way she wrote up every tally sheet the company ever had. She always used both sides of the paper, because paper costs money.

The first side you already know. *Beregost*, it says at the top, *third tenday of Mirtul*. That's about four months back. The company is wintering in rooms over a saddler's. They've taken a contract riding with iron wagons down to Nashkel and back. It pays poorly and steadily, and Dorna approves of steady. Brannoc's knee is worse. Little Fen married the saddler's daughter, *which solves the rent and creates other problems*. Everyone sends their regards, *except Orrin, who says you still owe him a gold piece from Saradush, and I have checked, and you do.*

Then the sheet turns over. This is where you stopped reading, wherever you were when you got it.

*Now the part I wrote this letter for.*

*Hollis went north to the Gate in the autumn. You'll remember the patriar debt from the Amnian job, the old house up the hill that hired us through a factor and then forgot to pay the back half. Hollis said he knew the name and knew the door and would collect it himself, and I let him, because he's Hollis and he usually does what he says.*

*He wrote once. A short letter from a tavern called the Blushing Mermaid, by the quays. He said the house wouldn't see him, and that the factor was dead or claimed to be. He said he'd had a run of bad luck at the Mermaid, though not at cards, he swore, and you know what that's worth from him. And he said not to worry, because he'd found steady work. Wet work, he called it. He said it paid better than the debt ever would.*

*That was the end of Eleint. Nothing since. Not for the winter, not for the spring, and Hollis always writes for the spring muster, even if it's just to say he isn't coming.*

*I'm not asking you to go. I know you're not with us anymore and I know why. But if the road ever takes you through the Gate, ask after him at the Mermaid. Someone there will know his face: grey in the beard, a notch out of the left ear, talks too much about birds. If he's drunk, tell him I'm cross. If he's in trouble, tell me. If it's worse, I'd rather know.*

*Look after yourself, James. Stop playing.*

*— D.H.*

Under the initials, smaller, as if she'd added it after the ink was dry:

*Orrin says the gold piece can wait.*

That's the whole letter. The candle has burned down another half-finger while you read. Downstairs the common room has gone quiet. A chair scrapes and a door bangs, and then it's just the well-rope creaking in its pulley.

The cat is still at the shutter. It has stood up now and is pressing its face to the crack, testing the gap with one whisker, then the other. Twice it glances past you at the bolted door. It doesn't seem to want anything from you. It's thinking about distances.

It's nearly one bell. Nothing else asks anything of you tonight. There's sleep, or anything else you'd rather do first.

Dorna's letter goes into the top flap of your pack, folded small and laid on top of everything else, where your hand will find it first whenever you open the pack.

The cat stays where it is at the shutter. You ease the wood closed past its nose, and the yard, the creaking well-rope and the night air from downhill are shut out. The latch drops.

Your thought reaches it. For a long moment nothing comes back. Then an answer comes, grudging and flat, like a paw lifted off a mouse it was sure of: *...yes.* Its tail lashes once against the floorboards. It keeps sitting with its face to the closed shutter, as if the wood might change its mind.

You pinch out the candle. The dark smells of tallow smoke and beeswax. Downstairs one last door bangs, the second stair creaks under somebody going up to bed, and after that there are only the small noises of an old house. Down by the water a ship's bell strikes the hour, and much later another one.

Some time in the night a weight lands on the end of the bed. The cat turns its circle and lies down at your feet, at the far end from the pack, with its back to it and its face to the door.

You wake to grey-gold light in the cracks of the shutter and the sound of the well: the rope running out, a bucket hitting water. In the yard below a woman tells a boy to mind his feet, in the voice of someone who has said it every morning for years. All over the city bells are ringing the hour, one after another and never quite together. You count nine. You slept the whole night through.

The cat is back at the shutter. When you stir, it turns its head and looks at you, and the bond carries one thing: *now.*

Someone knocks twice on the door.

"Jug's outside," Alan says through the wood. He doesn't walk off. The boards creak as he shifts his weight.

"Man came asking for you at first bell. Good coat, no colours on it. Asked if the gentleman from Tethyr was up yet." He pauses. "I didn't know you were from Tethyr. Didn't tell him you were, either. He offered me a silver for the room. I told him I don't know who's in which room. That's what I tell everybody."

The boards creak again.

"He said he'd call again. Toss is at ten bells, if you're still going up." Then, flatter: "Is he trouble I ought to keep out of my house?"

James draws the bolt and opens the door a hand's width. Alan stands in the narrow hall with his apron on and a dishcloth over one shoulder. The jug sits on the boards by his boot, beaded with cold from the well. The cat slips past your ankle, looks up at him, then sits down in the doorway as if it might be going somewhere.

At *downstairs, not up here* Alan nods once. "Downstairs suits me. The common room's got witnesses."

He thinks about your question the way he thought about the Watch last night, like a man pricing a cart ride.

"Forty, give or take. Clean-shaven. Grey coat, good wool, plain buttons, no badge or colours anywhere on him. Boots polished this morning, and splashed by the time he got here, so he walked down. Nobody walks down at first bell for pleasure." He shifts his weight. "He talks like up the hill, but he stood like a man who's used to waiting in other people's halls. Hands clean except for ink on the middle finger. He writes for someone, or he counts for them."

"No name. I asked. He said it wouldn't mean anything to you." Alan's mouth goes flat. "That's either true or rude. I didn't ask which."

"He asked when my guests come down to eat. I told him noon, more or less, because that's true of most of them." He looks at you, then at the cat in the doorway. "If he's back at noon and you're not, I'll tell him you're out. I won't say where, since I won't know."

From below, the street door bangs and someone calls for Alan. He lifts a hand in that direction without turning.

"Toss is in an hour." Then he's off down the hall, and the second stair creaks under him.

The jug is cold in your hands. All over the city the bells have stopped. The cat stays in the doorway, facing out toward the stairs, and through the bond it sends the same word as before, more patiently this time: *now.*

The morning is yours. There's the climb to the Lady's Hall for the ten-bell toss, the pull the cat is waiting on, or anything else.

You wash in the cold well water and it wakes you properly. Then you dress, fasten the regimental cloak at your throat and tuck the papers inside your coat against your ribs. Vane's note goes on top, with Dorna's letter folded small behind it. You keep the rod and the coin. The crossbow and the pack stay under the bed, and you lock the room behind you.

The cat doesn't wait for you on the stairs. It goes down ahead of you two treads at a time, tail straight up. It crosses the common room past Alan without a glance and is out the street door before you reach the bottom. Alan watches it go, then watches you follow, and says nothing. That's an answer of its own.

Outside, the Lower City is up and working. Carts are grinding up the hill, shutters are open, and the chandler from last night is hanging candles in bunches on his doorpost. The cat takes the same lane down that Tamsin took you up. It keeps to the gutter side, close to the walls, and every twenty paces or so it looks back to check you're still there. It does it with the air of something keeping a promise it didn't want to make.

By daylight the Counting House square is a different place. Clerks in dark coats climb the steps with satchels. A merchant argues with a porter about a strongbox. A pair of fresh halberdiers stand at the doors now, younger than last night's pair. The bucket and mop are gone from the side door. Your copper is still lying in the shadow of the first step, and two more lie beside it now. A clerk steps over all three without looking down.

The cat stops at the grate. It doesn't freeze this time. It sniffs at the bars once, briefly, the way you'd check a door you already know is locked, and then turns away from it. It goes along the foot of the Counting House wall, away from the steps, and into a gap between the building and the warehouse beside it. It's a stair-passage, barely wider than your shoulders, going down.

You follow. The stone steps are worn into dips and stay wet in the shade even at this hour. The Counting House wall rises sheer on your left, grey dressed stone like the front. About thirty feet down the stone changes. Below a line you could put your hand on, the courses are older and darker, with big blocks set without mortar and smoothed by something that isn't feet. The building is standing on someone else's foundations.

The stair ends at a small stone landing just above the harbour. There's no quay here, only a slimed ledge where the old wall goes down into the water. The tide is out, or most of the way out. Green weed hangs from the lower courses and drips, and the water slaps against the stone slowly and steadily. It's the same sound you heard through the grate last night, close enough now to wet your boots.

The cat goes to the last dry step and stops there. You can see it the whole time. It hasn't gone a whisker past where you said.

Through the bond: *Down.* Then a sharper pull, and it isn't toward the water. The cat's head turns, slow and deliberate, until its nose points at the old dark wall itself, back under the Counting House. *There. In. Wet.* After it comes the flat-eared feeling again, stronger than last night: *don't like. want.*

Set into the old wall, a foot above the waterline, is an iron mooring ring rusted to the colour of dried blood. Someone has tied a strip of red rag to it, knotted twice. The rag is bright and still stiff with dye. It hasn't been here long.

A gull lands on the ledge, looks at the cat, and thinks better of it.

Up above you, faintly, the bells start counting the half-hour toward ten.

You stay on the last dry step, where the cat is, and look the place over the way you'd once look over a ford before you sent men across it.

You don't need luck for the first part. People have been using this landing, and recently. The ring is rusted the colour of dried blood everywhere except one band on the inner curve, where it's been rubbed bright as a new nail. Rope has run through it under load more than once, and not long ago. A few tarred hemp fibres are still caught in the rust. The slime on the ledge below is churned, not smooth. It's been flattened into broad smears, and in one place there's a clear print of a bare heel, wide and flat. Whoever stood here came down without boots.

There's a smell too, under the weed and the brine. It's rancid and fatty, like old lard. On the stone beside the ring there's a dull grey smear, and it hasn't washed off because water doesn't take fat. People who swim cold water grease themselves before they go in.

Then there are the scratches. To the left of the ring, cut into the old dark stone with a knife point or a nail, is a short row of marks at different heights. Each is a little horizontal stroke, and some have a tiny notch beside them. The lowest sits right at the waterline. The highest is about a forearm's length above your boots. Someone stood here over and over and marked where the water came to.

Finding a way in is harder. You look along the courses below the ring for any join or gap or break in the masonry.

The wall won't give you a way in. Below the ring the old blocks go down into the green and vanish. The weed hangs over them in heavy wet curtains that sway with each slap of water, and every time you think you've found a darker line between two courses, the weed swings back across it. Under the surface the harbour is the colour of strong tea, and you can't see more than a hand's depth into it. If there's a door, a drain or a crack down there, the water is keeping it. All you can say for certain is that the blocks are huge and fitted without mortar, and that the stone is very old.

The cat doesn't care what you can see. It's still on the last dry step with its nose pointed at the same patch of dark wall, a little left of the ring and below the waterline. Through the bond comes the same pull again, impatient now: *There. In.* It flicks its tail once, at you or at the water, and doesn't move a whisker further.

Above you, faintly, someone starts down the Tallow Stair. Bare feet, or soft shoes, slapping on the wet steps. They're still well up, around the turn, out of sight.

The ten-bell toss at the Lady's Hall is half an hour off, and the climb takes most of that.

 You look the wall over course by course, from the ring down to the waterline, and you find no seam, no opening and no break in the stone. Whatever the cat is pointing at, you haven't found it.

*Beside.* The answer comes at once this time, without the sulk. The cat steps back off the last dry step and sits down against your boot, close enough that you can feel it through the leather. Its eyes stay on the turn of the stair.

The slapping footsteps get closer. Then they stop.

A boy stands at the turn about twenty feet above you, one hand flat on the Counting House wall. He's maybe twelve, barefoot, in sailcloth breeches rolled to the knee and a shirt that started out as someone else's. His feet are grey to the ankle with harbour mud. A coil of thin cord hangs over one shoulder, and a lump of lead the size of a plum is knotted to its end. He moves it behind his hip without seeming to notice he's done it.

He looks at you, at the cat, and then past you both. His eyes go to the mooring ring and the red rag for the length of a breath, and come back.

Through the bond the cat sends: *Small. Fast heart.* Then, after a pause: *Fish. Grease.*

The boy has made up his mind. He comes down three more steps, slowly, slouching as if he owns the stair, and stops where he can still turn and run.

"Morning, mister." The Lower City is thick in his voice, all dropped ends. "You lost? Nobody comes down the Tallow but rats and me." He tilts his head at the water. "If you dropped something off the top, it's gone. Mud takes it. I could look for you, though. Two coppers, I'll dive for it." He grins, and the grin doesn't reach any higher than his mouth. "What you after down here?"

Above him, out of sight, the bells finish counting the half-hour.

The boy looks at the cat for a long moment, as if he's never heard a stranger say anything so daft and isn't sure it's daft enough to be a lie.

"Your *cat*." His mouth twitches. "Cats go mad down the Tallow, mister. It's the fish. Gutters bring the heads down off the market and the gulls drop 'em here." He jerks his chin at the slime on the ledge. "Smells like dinner to him, that's all."

When you ask about a drain he answers too fast, before you've quite finished.

"No drain. Just wall." He shrugs with one shoulder, the one without the cord. "Old wall. Goes down, stops in the mud. Nothing comes out of it but crabs." He comes down one more step and stops there, still close enough to the turn to run. His eyes go to the mooring ring again, to the red rag and then to the row of knife-cut marks beside it, and come back to you more slowly. He's trying to work out whether you've seen them.

Under the slouch he keeps his weight on the balls of his feet. The cord's hidden behind his hip again, though he never seemed to move it, and he's holding the coil tight in one fist so the lead doesn't knock against the stone.

Against your boot the cat hasn't moved. The bond carries his heartbeat to you, quick and light, and one plain thing about the boy: *lying.* It's not a word so much as how prey holds still when it wants you to think it isn't there.

"Tide's on the turn," the boy says, and nods past you at the water without looking at it. "Comes up quick here, quicker than you'd think. Wets your boots, then your knees. You'd want to be up top before that." He makes it sound kindly meant. Then, just as kindly, he asks the thing he came down here to ask:

"You stoppin' near, mister? Never seen you on the quays before. Nor him."

Above you the Tallow Stair goes up wet and empty to its turn. It's twenty minutes, near enough, to ten bells.

Place: Old landing under the Counting House · Time: Day 2 · morning

The boy hears *yesterday* and *finding my way*, and his face doesn't change. You can see he's stored it away anyway. "Mind the third step from the top, mister," he says. "It's loose." He flattens his back against the Counting House wall to let you by. The cord is behind his hip again and his fist is still tight around the lead.

You keep to the outside edge of the stair and pass him without brushing his shoulder. The cat follows close at your heel, its tail low. At the turn it stops and looks back down once. Through the bond comes *small one, going down*. It isn't worried, only noting it. Behind you, bare feet slap quickly down toward the landing and the ring.

The third step from the top really is loose. It rocks under your boot and settles again.

The climb to the inner wall takes most of the half-hour, as you were told it would. Over the last stretch you're no longer climbing alone. A stream of people forms in the streets below the gate: a pair of clerks, a fishwife with her shawl pinned tight, a grandmother leading a boy in his feast-day collar on an ordinary day, two caravan guards still smelling of horse. Most of them carry a copper in their fingers, ready for after.

There are four of the Watch at the gate, in polished breastplates with their cloaks pinned back. The nearest calls "Toss?" to the stream of people, and the stream answers "Toss," ragged and good-humoured, the way it plainly does every morning. His eyes stop on your rapier, move up to your face and then take in the cat. The cat stares back without blinking. "Keep it sheathed up top," he says, and his gaze has already moved on to the caravan guards behind you.

The Upper City is quieter, cleaner and wider. The streets are swept, and there are gardens behind iron railings. The Lady's Hall stands at the head of a small plaza. It's tall and pale, with a dome sheathed in something that catches the sun, and the great doors are gilded as Tamsin said. Thirty or forty people gather at the foot of its steps. On the top step, in blue and silver, stands a priest of middle years with a broad, kindly face. He holds up a disc of gold the size of his palm so everyone can see it. At his elbow an old acolyte in plainer blue holds an open ledger against her chest, a pen ready in her other hand.

Ten bells begins all over the city.

On the last stroke the priest flips the coin. It goes up high, glittering, and turns and turns in the light. He catches it on the back of his left hand and covers it with his right. That moment is the whole art of the thing, and you've watched hands do it ten thousand times across ten thousand tables.

His right hand lifts away a heartbeat later than it needs to. Between the catch and the reveal his left thumb moves, a small roll under the covering palm. If you'd never done it yourself you'd take it for a man steadying the coin.

"The Lady smiles on the Gate," the priest says warmly, and turns his hand so the smiling face shows to the plaza.

The crowd sighs, pleased. A few of them flip their own coppers. The grandmother kisses hers and gives it to the boy.

The old acolyte lowers her eyes to the ledger. Her pen stays over the page for a long breath while the priest is still smiling at the crowd. Then it moves, and she writes something short.

At your boot the cat sits down and looks up at the gold disc as the priest slips it away into his sleeve. *Shiny,* it sends, and nothing more.

The crowd starts breaking up, some going back down toward the gate, some climbing the Hall's steps to go inside. Round the left flank of the building a smaller door stands open, with a young acolyte at a lectern and a book in front of him. That's the side door Alan told you about. The old woman with the ledger is following the priest in through the great doors.

My eyes linger on the shuffle a moment too long. I turn towards the tiefling lad instead, keeping my place in line.

I enjoyed James’s first night in the Gate. I’d come back for the next session—but I’d want a little less nudging and more confidence that the campaign files are being kept straight.

### What worked

- **The city felt inhabited.** Tamsin’s directions, Alan’s working bolt, the loose stair, the cleaning bucket: these were useful, grounded details, not just scenery.
- **NPC conversations rewarded attention.** Asking Tamsin about his name and later his mother produced my favourite exchange. I could be decent without it immediately becoming a reward transaction.
- **The mystery gave me things to investigate.** The note payable at the Counting House, its watermark, the tide marks, and the boy’s sounding line were concrete clues. The landing especially felt like the beginning of a heist: observe access, tides, and people before making a plan.
- **My choices were respected.** I could decline the cards, leave the landing, protect Tamsin’s confidence, and sleep. The failed Perception check didn’t halt the scene or force a reroll.
- **The cat had personality.** Its grudging cooperation and offended response to supper were excellent.

### What broke

**Record fidelity needs work.** The old-company letter was explicitly in the starting files, but I was initially asked to invent it. My out-of-game correction failed to send, though the letter eventually appeared. The starting records also changed Arcana to History and imposed attunement on the rod and cloak despite the campaign’s explicit exception. Some other changes look like attempts to correct the sheet to standard 5e; those should be explained and agreed, not silently substituted.

There was also a lore error: Tyche’s division belongs to the Dawn Cataclysm, not the Time of Troubles. Since that revelation came from a successful Religion check and appears central to the mystery, it matters.

### What was missing or overdone

**The guidance was too insistent.** The cat pointed toward the Counting House repeatedly; the copper, warm amulet, note, and watermark reinforced it. I understood the lead early. More space to choose how and when to pursue it would make following it feel more like my decision. The cat’s confident “lying” assessment also risks turning it into a truth detector rather than a familiar with limited perceptions.

The repeated assurances that “nothing else wants you tonight” felt like instructions to end the scene. I was still interested in my papers. Let the quiet stand without announcing what does or doesn’t matter.

Finally, the prose sometimes explained NPC emotions more certainly than James could know—particularly Tamsin’s history of being mistreated. His gestures and dialogue already conveyed plenty.

### Going forward

Keep the grounded conversations and actionable clues. Give James a clear initial understanding of Tymora’s job soon, then room to recruit and plan. Most importantly, keep discovered security facts stable. This opening made me want to investigate the Counting House; the payoff will be learning a place I can genuinely outthink, rather than following signals until its doors open.

Yes—when the barefoot boy went down to the landing after I left. I wanted to stop out of sight and watch what he did with the weighted cord and red rag. That felt like a chance to discover something through James’s scouting experience, rather than another supernatural hint.

I went to the Lady’s Hall instead because the repeated countdown to the toss made it feel like an appointment I shouldn’t miss. That was a legitimate choice with a time cost, not something you prevented—but I was more curious about the boy at that moment.

I also wanted to read the company letter when I first unpacked it. Being told it wasn’t in my inventory interrupted that impulse, and the failed out-of-game message made correcting it awkward. I did eventually get to do that, and the letter was worth reading.

“One night to start, supper and ale. If the bolt works and the cat behaves, we’ll discuss a longer arrangement.”

I count out ten silver and four copper onto the bar.

“James Worgen. And if I’m hoping to speak with someone from the Lady’s Hall tomorrow, is there a proper way to arrange it? I’d rather not spend the morning arguing theology with the Watch at the gate.”
turns.reply:
Alan watches the coins come down and counts them with his eyes before you've finished. Ten silver, four copper. He sweeps them off the bar into his palm without a word and drops them into a box under the counter.

"Worgen." He says it once, the way he'd chalk it on a slate. "One night. Supper, ale. Bolt works. You'll find out about the cat."

He takes an iron key on a loop of cord off a hook behind him and puts it on the bar in front of you. "Top of the stairs, left, all the way to the end. The door sticks in the wet. Shoulder it, don't kick it."

You ask about the Lady's Hall. He takes a moment over it, like a man working out the cost of a cart ride.

"Gates open at first bell. Go up clean and without the crossbow. The Watch stop a man with a weapon on his back, and they stop him longer if he talks like he's not from here." He nods at your rapier. "That on your hip, they'll look at it. They'll let it go if you're polite and going somewhere they like."

"Tell them you're going up for the morning toss. The priests flip a coin for the city at the Hall every morning, and half the Lower City climbs up to watch on a feast day. On an ordinary day it's a few dozen. The Watch are used to it, so it's the easy way through."

"Speaking to a priest is something else. You don't just walk up to one. There's a side door with an acolyte and a book. You give your name, leave something in the dish, and they find you a time. Leave a silver and they'll find you a time next week. Leave gold and they'll find one tomorrow." He shrugs. "I don't say that against the Lady. It's just how a big house runs."

He turns toward the kitchen hatch. "Hesta. One stew, back room."

A woman's voice answers from the steam, too low to make out. A minute later a bowl comes through the hatch: thick fish stew with the steam still rising off it, a heel of brown bread, and an apple, small and a little wrinkled but whole. Alan sets them in front of you with a tankard of ale, its foam already sliding down the side.

"You're lucky," he says, meaning the apple, and picks up the dry tankard again.

The cat comes out from under the stool, sits on the floor by your boot and looks at the stew, then at you. It makes no sound at all, and somehow that's worse than if it did.

Up near the beams Elf starts again, softer this time, a few low notes without words. At the fire table one of the Fist men loses a throw and swears at the dice, quite cheerfully.

Nothing else wants you tonight. There's supper, and a room at the end of the hall upstairs, unless you want something more from the evening.

“An apple already. Clearly I’ve come to the right city.”

I set aside a little fish to cool for the cat and eat my supper. Afterwards I take the key upstairs, let the cat in with me, and bolt the door.

turns.reply:
"Don't say that too loudly," Alan says, without looking up from the tankard. "Hesta will put the price up."

The stew is better than the price suggested: thick with white fish and onion, and peppery enough to make the ale welcome. You set a flake of fish on the edge of the bread to cool and lower it to the floor. The cat looks at it as if it has been insulted. Then it eats it in three neat bites and goes back to waiting for more. When none comes, it gives up on you and starts watching the door to the street instead.

By the fire the Fist men are counting up their losses. Up in the beams, Elf has gone quiet.

The stairs creak at every second tread. The hall at the top is narrow and smells of beeswax and old wood, and the door at the far left end sticks exactly as promised. You put a shoulder to it and it gives with a damp groan. The room is small and clean: a bed with a grey wool blanket, a stool, a washstand with an empty jug, and a tallow candle burning in a dish on the sill. The shutter is open a crack onto the yard. Below it the well-rope creaks in its pulley when the wind takes it. The cat comes in on your heel, and the bolt slides home with a solid, well-oiled *chock*. Alan was telling the truth about that too.

You lay your papers out on the blanket by candlelight.

The promissory note is heavy paper, the kind a patriar's clerk uses, not a dockside scribe. It's cream-coloured and still crisp at the folds even after the voyage. The hand is young, and it hurries the way a man writes when the table is waiting on him:

*I, Peregrin Vane, of House Vane of Baldur's Gate, owe the bearer of this paper four hundred gold pieces, to be paid on presentation at the Counting House of Baldur's Gate, against the account of my House.*

Below that is the signature, *P. Vane*, with a flourish that has run out of ink halfway. A small blind stamp is pressed into the corner without wax: a weathervane, a little arrow on a crossed post, pointing nowhere in particular. Where the place and date should be, someone has set a wine cup down. A brown ring has eaten the line, and only *-ember* and a scrap of a number are left.

So it's the Counting House again.

The candle is behind the sheet as you tilt it to read the stamp. For a moment the paper isn't even. There's a paler patch in the middle of the weave, a shape the size of a thumbprint that's thinner than the rest. It's gone as you lower the page, and at this angle you can't make out what it was.

The cat jumps onto the bed. It treads a slow circle on the blanket the way cats do when they're choosing a place to settle, and stops on the edge of the note. It lifts the paw back off the paper as if the paper were wet. Then it steps around it, all the way around, and lies down on the far side of the bed with its back to the note.

A minute later it gets up again and goes to the shutter. It sits at the crack with its nose to the night air, facing downhill.

At one angle the pale patch is only a smudge in the weave. Tilt it a little further and it takes shape.

It's a face, about the size of a thumbprint, pressed into the body of the paper. Whoever made it put it there when the sheet was still wet pulp on the mould, not with ink. It's a woman's face, looking straight at you, set inside a thin ring of tiny raised marks, the way a face sits inside the rim of a coin. The work is fine. You can make out the line of her brows, the curve of her cheek and the shape of her mouth.

Her mouth turns down. Under each eye a short line runs across the cheek, thinner than a hair. The paper is translucent there, so in this light it shines. She is weeping.

The words *four hundred gold pieces* run straight across her face, with the ink stroke of *gold* passing between her eyes. The paper-maker can't have planned that. The clerk who wrote on it can't have known.

Behind you, at the shutter, the cat has turned its head. It doesn't come back to the bed. turns.message: I lay the note flat beside my coin of Tymora and compare the watermark’s face with the Lady’s profile, trying to recall whether I’ve seen that weeping face or its surrounding marks in any religious imagery before.
turns.reply:
You unfold the note on the grey blanket and smooth it flat with the side of your hand. You lift the cord over your head and lay the Coin of Tymora beside it, close enough to touch.

Laid flat, the paper gives you nothing. It's just cream-coloured weave with Peregrin Vane's hurried hand across it and the wine ring in the corner. The face only comes up when there's light behind it, so you have to compare from what you saw a minute ago, with the coin under the candle.

Your coin is old Tethyrian-struck silver, worn almost smooth. The Lady is in profile, looking left, and you can still make out a curl of hair and the lift at the corner of her mouth. A ring of tiny beads runs round the rim, the kind mints put there so clippers can't shave the edge without it showing.

The watermark's face looked straight out at you, not in profile. Its ring of marks was finer than your coin's beading, and irregular. Some were round and some were short strokes, as if they were meant to say something.

You turn it over in your mind, trying to place where you've seen it before: temple friezes in Tethyr, shrine-coins sold on pilgrim roads, the coins the chaplains carried in Zaranda's camps.

The answer comes, though not from anything you've seen on a temple wall.

It isn't the Lady. Nobody who serves Tymora shows her weeping, not in stone, not on coins, not in a chaplain's scratched drawing. Her face smiles or it's not hers. It isn't Beshaba either. The Maid of Misfortune's people don't carve a woman's face at all. Their sign is black antlers on red, and they don't put it on anything a respectable mill would make.

The lore you're remembering is older than both of them. Before the Time of Troubles there was one goddess of luck, not two. Tyche, the old priests called her. When the gods walked the earth she was split in two: Tymora came out of her smiling, and Beshaba came out of her bitter. Coins of Tyche's faith were struck with the same woman on both faces, fair on one side and foul on the other. Her people flipped them for their answers, and when they kept one as a charm they kept it smile-up. Old Tymoran clergy still talk about those coins like a family talks about a grandmother nobody mentions at the table.

So the face in Vane's paper looks like the bad side of that kind of coin. It's set inside a rim, the way a mint would strike it, and it's weeping.

What you don't recognise is the ring of marks around it. On a temple coin the rim would carry a prayer or the name of a mint. These look like neither: rounds and short strokes in no script you know, too regular to be decoration. A paper-maker pressed them into the mould on purpose.

The paper itself doesn't add up. A mill picks what goes in its moulds, and no patriar house would order the foul face of a luck-coin for its letters of credit. That leaves two possibilities: someone wanted it there, or nobody did.

The Coin of Tymora lies beside the note in the candlelight, worn and silver and cool now.

At the shutter the cat hasn't moved. Its nose is still at the crack and its tail still tight round its feet. Every so often one ear turns toward the door of the room and then back toward the yard, as if it's measuring how far it is to somewhere.

The candle has burned down maybe a finger's width since you came up. The night is quiet. Nothing else is waiting on you before sleep unless you want it.

I slip Tymora’s coin back around my neck and fold the note carefully away.

“Tomorrow we’ll ask someone who knows,” I tell the cat. “Preferably before we start climbing down drains.”

I settle on the bed and open the unfinished letter from the Copper Lanterns, reading it through by candlelight.

The coin goes back on its cord and settles against your breastbone, cool now. The note goes back into its fold and into the pack. The cat doesn't look round when you speak to it. One ear turns toward you and then back toward the yard. Something about *drains* gets a flick of the tail, and that's all.

The Copper Lanterns letter has been folded and unfolded so often that it's gone soft along the creases, like cloth. It's Dorna Hask's hand, small, square and leaning slightly backward, the way she wrote up every tally sheet the company ever had. She always used both sides of the paper, because paper costs money.

The first side you already know. *Beregost*, it says at the top, *third tenday of Mirtul*. That's about four months back. The company is wintering in rooms over a saddler's. They've taken a contract riding with iron wagons down to Nashkel and back. It pays poorly and steadily, and Dorna approves of steady. Brannoc's knee is worse. Little Fen married the saddler's daughter, *which solves the rent and creates other problems*. Everyone sends their regards, *except Orrin, who says you still owe him a gold piece from Saradush, and I have checked, and you do.*

Then the sheet turns over. This is where you stopped reading, wherever you were when you got it.

*Now the part I wrote this letter for.*

*Hollis went north to the Gate in the autumn. You'll remember the patriar debt from the Amnian job, the old house up the hill that hired us through a factor and then forgot to pay the back half. Hollis said he knew the name and knew the door and would collect it himself, and I let him, because he's Hollis and he usually does what he says.*

*He wrote once. A short letter from a tavern called the Blushing Mermaid, by the quays. He said the house wouldn't see him, and that the factor was dead or claimed to be. He said he'd had a run of bad luck at the Mermaid, though not at cards, he swore, and you know what that's worth from him. And he said not to worry, because he'd found steady work. Wet work, he called it. He said it paid better than the debt ever would.*

*That was the end of Eleint. Nothing since. Not for the winter, not for the spring, and Hollis always writes for the spring muster, even if it's just to say he isn't coming.*

*I'm not asking you to go. I know you're not with us anymore and I know why. But if the road ever takes you through the Gate, ask after him at the Mermaid. Someone there will know his face: grey in the beard, a notch out of the left ear, talks too much about birds. If he's drunk, tell him I'm cross. If he's in trouble, tell me. If it's worse, I'd rather know.*

*Look after yourself, James. Stop playing.*

*— D.H.*

Under the initials, smaller, as if she'd added it after the ink was dry:

*Orrin says the gold piece can wait.*

That's the whole letter. The candle has burned down another half-finger while you read. Downstairs the common room has gone quiet. A chair scrapes and a door bangs, and then it's just the well-rope creaking in its pulley.

The cat is still at the shutter. It has stood up now and is pressing its face to the crack, testing the gap with one whisker, then the other. Twice it glances past you at the bolted door. It doesn't seem to want anything from you. It's thinking about distances.

It's nearly one bell. Nothing else asks anything of you tonight. There's sleep, or anything else you'd rather do first.

Then I go to the shutter and gently close it. *Not alone tonight,* I tell the cat through the bond. *I’ll follow this with you tomorrow. I promise.*

The cat stays where it is at the shutter. You ease the wood closed past its nose, and the yard, the creaking well-rope and the night air from downhill are shut out. The latch drops.

Your thought reaches it. For a long moment nothing comes back. Then an answer comes, grudging and flat, like a paw lifted off a mouse it was sure of: *...yes.* Its tail lashes once against the floorboards. It keeps sitting with its face to the closed shutter, as if the wood might change its mind.

You pinch out the candle. The dark smells of tallow smoke and beeswax. Downstairs one last door bangs, the second stair creaks under somebody going up to bed, and after that there are only the small noises of an old house. Down by the water a ship's bell strikes the hour, and much later another one.

Some time in the night a weight lands on the end of the bed. The cat turns its circle and lies down at your feet, at the far end from the pack, with its back to it and its face to the door.

You wake to grey-gold light in the cracks of the shutter and the sound of the well: the rope running out, a bucket hitting water. In the yard below a woman tells a boy to mind his feet, in the voice of someone who has said it every morning for years. All over the city bells are ringing the hour, one after another and never quite together. You count nine. You slept the whole night through.

The cat is back at the shutter. When you stir, it turns its head and looks at you, and the bond carries one thing: *now.*

Someone knocks twice on the door.

"Jug's outside," Alan says through the wood. He doesn't walk off. The boards creak as he shifts his weight.

"Man came asking for you at first bell. Good coat, no colours on it. Asked if the gentleman from Tethyr was up yet." He pauses. "I didn't know you were from Tethyr. Didn't tell him you were, either. He offered me a silver for the room. I told him I don't know who's in which room. That's what I tell everybody."

The boards creak again.

"He said he'd call again. Toss is at ten bells, if you're still going up." Then, flatter: "Is he trouble I ought to keep out of my house?"

I get up and open the door enough to speak quietly with Alan.

The jug sits on the boards by his boot, beaded with cold from the well. The cat slips past your ankle, looks up at him, then sits down in the doorway as if it might be going somewhere.

At *downstairs, not up here* Alan nods once. "Downstairs suits me. The common room's got witnesses."

He thinks about your question the way he thought about the Watch last night, like a man pricing a cart ride.

"Forty, give or take. Clean-shaven. Grey coat, good wool, plain buttons, no badge or colours anywhere on him. Boots polished this morning, and splashed by the time he got here, so he walked down. Nobody walks down at first bell for pleasure." He shifts his weight. "He talks like up the hill, but he stood like a man who's used to waiting in other people's halls. Hands clean except for ink on the middle finger. He writes for someone, or he counts for them."

"No name. I asked. He said it wouldn't mean anything to you." Alan's mouth goes flat. "That's either true or rude. I didn't ask which."

"He asked when my guests come down to eat. I told him noon, more or less, because that's true of most of them." He looks at you, then at the cat in the doorway. "If he's back at noon and you're not, I'll tell him you're out. I won't say where, since I won't know."

From below, the street door bangs and someone calls for Alan. He lifts a hand in that direction without turning.

"Toss is in an hour." Then he's off down the hall, and the second stair creaks under him.

The jug is cold in your hands. All over the city the bells have stopped. The cat stays in the doorway, facing out toward the stairs, and through the bond it sends the same word as before, more patiently this time: *now.*

The morning is yours. There's the climb to the Lady's Hall for the ten-bell toss, the pull the cat is waiting on, or anything else.

*Yes. Now. But stay where I can see you—no slipping underground without me.*

turns.reply:
You wash in the cold well water and it wakes you properly. Then you dress, fasten the regimental cloak at your throat and tuck the papers inside your coat against your ribs. Vane's note goes on top, with Dorna's letter folded small behind it. You keep the rod and the coin. The crossbow and the pack stay under the bed, and you lock the room behind you.

The cat doesn't wait for you on the stairs. It goes down ahead of you two treads at a time, tail straight up. It crosses the common room past Alan without a glance and is out the street door before you reach the bottom. Alan watches it go, then watches you follow, and says nothing. That's an answer of its own.

Outside, the Lower City is up and working. Carts are grinding up the hill, shutters are open, and the chandler from last night is hanging candles in bunches on his doorpost. The cat takes the same lane down that Tamsin took you up. It keeps to the gutter side, close to the walls, and every twenty paces or so it looks back to check you're still there. It does it with the air of something keeping a promise it didn't want to make.

By daylight the Counting House square is a different place. Clerks in dark coats climb the steps with satchels. A merchant argues with a porter about a strongbox. A pair of fresh halberdiers stand at the doors now, younger than last night's pair. The bucket and mop are gone from the side door. Your copper is still lying in the shadow of the first step, and two more lie beside it now. A clerk steps over all three without looking down.

The cat stops at the grate. It doesn't freeze this time. It sniffs at the bars once, briefly, the way you'd check a door you already know is locked, and then turns away from it. It goes along the foot of the Counting House wall, away from the steps, and into a gap between the building and the warehouse beside it. It's a stair-passage, barely wider than your shoulders, going down.

You follow. The stone steps are worn into dips and stay wet in the shade even at this hour. The Counting House wall rises sheer on your left, grey dressed stone like the front. About thirty feet down the stone changes. Below a line you could put your hand on, the courses are older and darker, with big blocks set without mortar and smoothed by something that isn't feet. The building is standing on someone else's foundations.

The stair ends at a small stone landing just above the harbour. There's no quay here, only a slimed ledge where the old wall goes down into the water. The tide is out, or most of the way out. Green weed hangs from the lower courses and drips, and the water slaps against the stone slowly and steadily. It's the same sound you heard through the grate last night, close enough now to wet your boots.

The cat goes to the last dry step and stops there. You can see it the whole time. It hasn't gone a whisker past where you said.

Through the bond: *Down.* Then a sharper pull, and it isn't toward the water. The cat's head turns, slow and deliberate, until its nose points at the old dark wall itself, back under the Counting House. *There. In. Wet.* After it comes the flat-eared feeling again, stronger than last night: *don't like. want.*

Set into the old wall, a foot above the waterline, is an iron mooring ring rusted to the colour of dried blood. Someone has tied a strip of red rag to it, knotted twice. The rag is bright and still stiff with dye. It hasn't been here long.

A gull lands on the ledge, looks at the cat, and thinks better of it.

Up above you, faintly, the bells start counting the half-hour toward ten.

You don't need luck for the first part. People have been using this landing, and recently. The ring is rusted the colour of dried blood everywhere except one band on the inner curve, where it's been rubbed bright as a new nail. Rope has run through it under load more than once, and not long ago. A few tarred hemp fibres are still caught in the rust. The slime on the ledge below is churned, not smooth. It's been flattened into broad smears, and in one place there's a clear print of a bare heel, wide and flat. Whoever stood here came down without boots.

There's a smell too, under the weed and the brine. It's rancid and fatty, like old lard. On the stone beside the ring there's a dull grey smear, and it hasn't washed off because water doesn't take fat. People who swim cold water grease themselves before they go in.

Then there are the scratches. To the left of the ring, cut into the old dark stone with a knife point or a nail, is a short row of marks at different heights. Each is a little horizontal stroke, and some have a tiny notch beside them. The lowest sits right at the waterline. The highest is about a forearm's length above your boots. Someone stood here over and over and marked where the water came to.

Finding a way in is harder. You look along the courses below the ring for any join or gap or break in the masonry.

The wall won't give you a way in. Below the ring the old blocks go down into the green and vanish. The weed hangs over them in heavy wet curtains that sway with each slap of water, and every time you think you've found a darker line between two courses, the weed swings back across it. Under the surface the harbour is the colour of strong tea, and you can't see more than a hand's depth into it. If there's a door, a drain or a crack down there, the water is keeping it. All you can say for certain is that the blocks are huge and fitted without mortar, and that the stone is very old.

The cat doesn't care what you can see. It's still on the last dry step with its nose pointed at the same patch of dark wall, a little left of the ring and below the waterline. Through the bond comes the same pull again, impatient now: *There. In.* It flicks its tail once, at you or at the water, and doesn't move a whisker further.

Above you, faintly, someone starts down the Tallow Stair. Bare feet, or soft shoes, slapping on the wet steps. They're still well up, around the turn, out of sight.

The ten-bell toss at the Lady's Hall is half an hour off, and the climb takes most of that.

 You look the wall over course by course, from the ring down to the waterline, and you find no seam, no opening and no break in the stone. Whatever the cat is pointing at, you haven't found it.

*Stay beside me,* I tell the cat.

I straighten and turn towards the stair, keeping my hands relaxed and clear of my weapons. I wait to see who’s coming down.
turns.reply:
*Beside.* The answer comes at once this time, without the sulk. The cat steps back off the last dry step and sits down against your boot, close enough that you can feel it through the leather. Its eyes stay on the turn of the stair.

The slapping footsteps get closer. Then they stop.

A boy stands at the turn about twenty feet above you, one hand flat on the Counting House wall. He's maybe twelve, barefoot, in sailcloth breeches rolled to the knee and a shirt that started out as someone else's. His feet are grey to the ankle with harbour mud. A coil of thin cord hangs over one shoulder, and a lump of lead the size of a plum is knotted to its end. He moves it behind his hip without seeming to notice he's done it.

He looks at you, at the cat, and then past you both. His eyes go to the mooring ring and the red rag for the length of a breath, and come back.

Through the bond the cat sends: *Small. Fast heart.* Then, after a pause: *Fish. Grease.*

The boy has made up his mind. He comes down three more steps, slowly, slouching as if he owns the stair, and stops where he can still turn and run.

"Morning, mister." The Lower City is thick in his voice, all dropped ends. "You lost? Nobody comes down the Tallow but rats and me." He tilts his head at the water. "If you dropped something off the top, it's gone. Mud takes it. I could look for you, though. Two coppers, I'll dive for it." He grins, and the grin doesn't reach any higher than his mouth. "What you after down here?"

Above him, out of sight, the bells finish counting the half-hour.

I glance at the water, then back at the boy.

His eyes go to the mooring ring again, to the red rag and then to the row of knife-cut marks beside it, and come back to you more slowly. He's trying to work out whether you've seen them.

Under the slouch he keeps his weight on the balls of his feet. The cord's hidden behind his hip again, though he never seemed to move it, and he's holding the coil tight in one fist so the lead doesn't knock against the stone.
